caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Tunisia's debt has more than doubled as a share of GDP in a decade of political turmoil and stalled reform. From 38.8% in 2010, the series low, it climbed through the post-revolution years as tourism collapsed and the wage bill ballooned: 85.7% in 2024, the series high, easing to a projected 81.2% in 2025. Tunisia has relied on domestic banks to absorb issuance, creating a dangerous sovereign-bank nexus, and has repeatedly sought but failed to complete IMF programs, most recently stalling over subsidy and wage reforms the Saied government rejects. At 81% of GDP with no market access and no IMF anchor, Tunisia is financing itself hand-to-mouth.
inflation_management: Tunisia's inflation crept upward through the 2010s as the dinar depreciated and subsidies were partially adjusted: from 3.2% in 2011, the series low, to 7.3% in 2018. The 2022 global shock and drought pushed it to 8.3% in 2022 and a series high of 9.3% in 2023. The central bank hiked rates and held them high, bringing inflation down to 7.0% in 2024 and a projected 5.3% in 2025. But monetary policy fights with one hand tied: administered prices and subsidies suppress measured inflation while distorting the economy, and the real adjustment is suppressed through shortages and arrears rather than prices.

key_events.event: Revolution ousted Ben Ali (January 2011); tourism and investment collapsed.
Democratic transition completed with a new constitution; IMF programs began and stalled repeatedly.
President Kais Saied elected; then seized emergency powers (July 2021), suspending parliament.
New constitution concentrated power; IMF $1.9bn deal agreed in principle (2022) but never completed.
Saied re-elected (October 2024) amid crackdown on opposition; debt hit 85.7% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued stagnation: debt near 80% of GDP, inflation near 5-7%, and growth too low to stabilize either without reforms the government refuses. Upside requires an IMF program and subsidy reform; downside is a disorderly debt event as domestic banks reach their absorption limits. Uncertainty is high: Tunisia's crisis is political, and the economics will not stabilize before the politics do.
